Remember that the **identity matrix** $I_n$ is an $n \times n$ square matrix with $1$'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are $0.$ For example, the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix $I_3$ is given below:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged.

For example, let's consider the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}
$$

Multiplying the matrix $A$ by the identity matrix $I_3,$ we find that the result is just $A$ itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot {I}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-2)\cdot 1+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 1 \\ 6\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\ 23\cdot 1+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A \cdot I_3 = A.$ You can check that $I_3 \cdot A = A$ using the same method.

This result holds in general: 

> For *any* square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ we have
> 
> 
> $$
> A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A.
> $$

In other words, the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$ has a similar property to the number $1,$ namely that 

$$
a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a
$$

 for any real number $a.$

Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$

For example, consider the matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$

Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$

On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/f7/f7c16deb083b467c063c900196274d08c532ad4633354f375530cb2cbe270491.png)

What is the image of this triangle under the action of the transformation  $\mathbf{T}$ represented by the matrix 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

To find the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we first create a matrix $X$ containing all vertices of our triangle written as columns:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,0).$ Notice that these points lie on the same line. Two of them even coincide!

So, the image of our triangle under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the following line segment:

![](images/88/88383b8eca1805c158f80d998d844d4c666b15d118a0ec26b4a1ba43c781fc76.png)

Note the following:

This is an example of a linear transformation that does not preserve linear independence. 

* First, notice that since [math]\det(T)= 0,[/math] the matrix [math]T[/math] is singular, which means that the vectors represented by the columns of [math] T,[/math] given below, are *not* linearly independent. 
\[
\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \:  \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right\}
\]  

- Recall that for any linear transformation $\mathbf T$ and region $D,$ we have 

$$
\text{Area}(\mathbf{T}(D)) = |\det(T)| \cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

 
Since $|\det(T)|  = 0$ in this case, any object applied to $\mathbf T$ collapses to an object with zero area.

- Also, the fact that $|\det(T)|  = 0$ tells us that $\mathbf T$ has no inverse transformation. Therefore, it is impossible to recover the original triangle knowing only its image and the matrix $T.$

Given a linear transformation $\mathbf T$ with an associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ there are three possibilities regarding the type of object formed under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ by a two-dimensional preimage. 

To demonstrate, consider the three-sided polygon $\mathcal P$ with vertices $(0,1)$, $(2,0)$ and $(2,1),$ as shown below. 

![](images/97/97689c7aaf7f6d42314fd01cb36b557df8081880659bcea08905e6c57f358ac1.png)

Let's describe the three possible types of object formed by the image of $\mathcal P{:}$

- Case where $T$ is non-singular:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can easily check that $T$ is non-singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $\mathcal P$ and then compute the product $TX{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a triangle.

![](images/14/145753e4f69dfa67bb45f59b7e9ed8bca789c589d4c5340ce2112363fa70cd7b.png)

- Case where $\mathbf{T}$ is singular and has at least one nonzero entry:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can easily check that $T$ is singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 3-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 4 & 10 \\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of  $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

![](images/46/46d387dbf6678d324135dbbb3439688c0bdbf9f9567baef56f34aa4aa9ee22e3.png)

- Case where $T$ is the zero matrix:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation represented by the zero matrix:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Clearly, $T$ is singular. Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are all $(0,0)$, the origin $O$ of the coordinate system.

![](images/97/97689c7aaf7f6d42314fd01cb36b557df8081880659bcea08905e6c57f358ac1.png)

Let's describe the three possible types of object formed by the image of $\mathcal P{:}$

- Case where $T$ is non-singular:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

$$
T = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can easily check that $T$ is non-singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $\mathcal P$ and then compute the product $TX{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a triangle.

![](images/14/145753e4f69dfa67bb45f59b7e9ed8bca789c589d4c5340ce2112363fa70cd7b.png)

- Case where $\mathbf{T}$ is singular and has at least one nonzero entry:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation with the following matrix representation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can easily check that $T$ is singular by computing its determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 3-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 4 & 10 \\ 3 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of  $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

![](images/46/46d387dbf6678d324135dbbb3439688c0bdbf9f9567baef56f34aa4aa9ee22e3.png)

- Case where $T$ is the zero matrix:

Let $\mathbf T$ be the linear transformation represented by the zero matrix:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Clearly, $T$ is singular. Now, computing the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the image's vertices are all $(0,0)$, the origin $O$ of the coordinate system.

$$

In a simple undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $m$ vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$ and $n$ edges $e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n$, the **incidence matrix** $B$ is an $m \times n$ matrix (table), where the entry at the intersection of the $i$th row and the $j$th column equals:

- $1$, if the vertex $v_i$ is incident to the edge $e_j$;
- $0$, otherwise.

In multigraphs, each loop contributes $2$ to the corresponding entry since the edge is incident to the vertex twice.

As we know, graphs can be represented graphically in various equally valid ways. In contrast, once we have fixed orderings of the vertices and of the edges, the incidence matrix of a graph is unique.

Consider the graph below.

![](images/0f/0fc2a8670607edc909c87c41371e102ff4901bab9309fde74d8f0837b09418e4.png)

Let's examine the vertices $v_1,v_2$, and $v_3$ of the graph to determine the entries of the incidence matrix.

- The vertex $v_1$ is incident to the edges $e_1$ and $e_2$. Hence, we write $1$ in the $1$st and $2$nd columns of the $1$st row, and $0$ in the other columns.

|  | $e_1$ | $e_2$ | $e_3$ | $e_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $v_2$ |  |  |  |  |
| $v_3$ |  |  |  |  |

- The vertex $v_2$ is incident to the edges $e_1, e_2$, and $e_3$. Hence, we write $1$ in the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns of the $2$nd row, and $0$ in the $4$th column.

|  | $e_1$ | $e_2$ | $e_3$ | $e_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $v_2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $v_3$ |  |  |  |  |

- The vertex $v_3$ is incident to the edge $e_3$ and also to the loop formed by $e_4$. Hence, we write $1$ in the $3$rd column of the $3$rd row, $2$ in the $4$th column to indicate the loop, and $0$ in the other columns.

|  | $e_1$ | $e_2$ | $e_3$ | $e_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row. 

Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use *any* row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a **Laplace expansion**.

Across the row $i,$ the Laplace expansion of an $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A$ is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{ij}{C}_{ij} \\  & ={a}_{i1}{C}_{i1}+{a}_{i2}{C}_{i2}+⋯+{a}_{in}{C}_{in},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\color{blue}C_{ij}}$ is the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ in $A.$ Remember the cofactor of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ is 

$$
{\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},
$$

where ${\color{black}M_{ij}}$ is the minor of the entry.

For example, consider the following matrix:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ($i=3$) as follows:

![](images/6e/6e8d5f7f4111e8963a6d4c7daf2bd5116d8099e18f41c53f2dae73f659f01e35.svg)

So, we reduced a $4 \times 4$ determinant to a $3 \times 3$ determinant.

Every linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ that acts on 2D-vectors has a $2 \times 2$ matrix $T$ associated with it. The matrix is called the **standard matrix** of the linear transformation. 
For any vector $\mathbf{v},$ the standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ must have the property

$$
\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = T \cdot \mathbf{v}
$$

where $T \cdot \mathbf{v}$ is the matrix product of the standard matrix $T$ and the vector $\mathbf{v}.$

To illustrate, consider the following linear transformation:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}
$$

The standard matrix for the linear transformation $\mathbf{S}$ is $\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 7 \\ 1 & -5\end{bmatrix}$ since it has the following property:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{S}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 7 \\ 1 & -5\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3\cdot x+7\cdot y \\ 1\cdot x+(-5)\cdot y\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3x+7y \\ x-5y\end{bmatrix} \\  & =S\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice here that $\mathbf{S}$ (using a **bold** letter) denotes the transformation (function) itself, while $S$ (big *italic* letter) is a $2 \times 2$ matrix that corresponds to the linear transformation.

In general, the standard matrix of the linear transformation $\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}$ is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{bmatrix}
$$

We can learn a lot about linear transformations by looking at their standard matrices.

In an undirected graph, $a_{ij}$ is always equal to $a_{ji}$; that is, the adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric about the main diagonal.

As we know, graphs can be represented graphically in various equally valid ways. In contrast, if we fix an ordering on the vertices, the adjacency matrix is unique.

- There is a loop at $v_1$. Hence, we write $2$ at the entry $a_{11}$, which is at the intersection of the 1st row and the 1st column. Since there are no loops at $v_2$ and $v_3$, we write $0$ at the entries $a_{22}$ and $a_{33}$.

$$

$$
A^3 = A \times A \times A
$$

and then examine the entry $(A^3)_{24}$ of the result.

I. - $P(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_2^2$
II. - $Q(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_1x_3+x_2^2$

Let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- $P(\mathbf{x})$ is in canonical form. Indeed, the form does not contain any cross-product terms (it contains only squares).

- $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is *not* in canonical form since it contains the cross-product term $2x_1x_3.$

In terms of matrix representation 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

 we have a canonical form if the corresponding matrix $A$ is diagonal.

For example, which of the following quadratic forms are given in their canonical forms?

I. - $R(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},$ where $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
II. - $S(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},$ where $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$

Examining our quadratic forms, we obtain the following.

- $R(\mathbf{x})$ is in canonical form. Indeed, its corresponding matrix is diagonal.

- $S(\mathbf{x})$ is *not* in canonical form since its corresponding matrix is not diagonal.

When a $2\times 2$ matrix with repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ is not diagonalizable, its Jordan canonical form is given by

$$
J = J_2(\lambda).
$$

As an example, let's find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}5 & 4 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

We first find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\det(A-\lambda I)=0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ -1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ 

Since $A$ has a repeated eigenvalue and is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable. 

Therefore, in this case, the Jordan canonical form of $A$ is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Note that $J$ is "almost" diagonal.

Given a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ we have $3$ possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2,$ then $A$ is diagonalizable, and $J$ is a diagonal matrix. In this case, $J$ is a composition of two distinct $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- If $A$ has only one eigenvalue $\lambda$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$ and there exist two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, then $A$ must be a scalar matrix. $$
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

- If $A$ has only one eigenvalue $\lambda$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$ and only one linearly independent eigenvector exists that corresponds to this eigenvalue, then $A$ is not diagonalizable. In this case, $J$ is a single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}
$$

So, in two out of three cases, our matrix is diagonalizable. But in the third case, the closest we can get to a diagonal matrix is a Jordan block with a $1$ on the superdiagonal.

In a directed multigraph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$, the **adjacency matrix** $A$ of the graph is an $n \times n$ matrix (table), where the entry $a_{ij}$ at the intersection of the $i$th row and the $j$th column equals the number of edges from $v_i$ to $v_j$ (in this order).

Notice that, according to this definition:

- If there are no edges connecting $v_i$ and $v_j$, the corresponding entry is $0$.
- For $i=j$, we count the number of loops at the vertex $v_i$.
- The adjacency matrix of a directed graph is *not* symmetric in general.

Let's look at an example of how to build the adjacency matrix for the graph below.

![](images/ef/ef213f4c4dda9a2622acc399327941a3e531188debe8d6c03d40e3f456cd6fee.png)

Let's examine the edges of the graph to determine the matrix entries step by step.

- There is an edge from $v_1$ to $v_2$. Hence, we write $1$ in the entry $a_{12}$.

|  | $v_1$ | $v_2$ | $v_3$ | $v_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ |  | $1$ |  |  |
| $v_2$ |  |  |  |  |
| $v_3$ |  |  |  |  |
| $v_4$ |  |  |  |  |

- There are two edges from $v_2$ to $v_3$. Hence, we write $2$ in the entry $a_{23}$.

|  | $v_1$ | $v_2$ | $v_3$ | $v_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ |  | $1$ |  |  |
| $v_2$ |  |  | $2$ |  |
| $v_3$ |  |  |  |  |
| $v_4$ |  |  |  |  |

- There is an edge from $v_4$ to $v_4$ (i.e., the loop). Hence, we write $1$ in the entry $a_{44}$.

|  | $v_1$ | $v_2$ | $v_3$ | $v_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ |  | $1$ |  |  |
| $v_2$ |  |  | $2$ |  |
| $v_3$ |  |  |  |  |
| $v_4$ |  |  |  | $1$ |

- Finally, we write $0$ for all remaining entries where no edges exist.

|  | $v_1$ | $v_2$ | $v_3$ | $v_4$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $v_1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $v_2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $2$ | $0$ |
| $v_3$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $v_4$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ |

The adjacency matrix is completed. In the usual matrix notation, we can write this as follows.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

If two matrices $A$ and $B$ have the same size, we can define a new matrix where each entry is the product of the corresponding entries in $A$ and $B$.

We write the Hadamard product using the symbol $\odot$.
Suppose we have two $n \times m$ matrices

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a_{11} & a_{12} & ⋯ & a_{1m} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} & ⋯ & a_{2m} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ a_{n1} & a_{n2} & ⋯ & a_{nm}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Once we know how to compute the Hadamard product entry by entry, it’s helpful to understand how it behaves algebraically.

If $A, B, C \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, then the Hadamard product satisfies the following properties:

- **Commutativity**
$A \odot B = B \odot A$
Element-wise multiplication doesn’t depend on order.
- **Associativity**
$(A \odot B) \odot C = A \odot (B \odot C)$
We can group Hadamard products however we like.
- **Distributivity over Addition**
$A \odot (B + C) = A \odot B + A \odot C$
This works just like normal multiplication, distributing over addition, but entry by entry.
- **Scalar Distributivity**
$\alpha(A \odot B) = (\alpha A) \odot B = A \odot (\alpha B)$
Scaling before or after the Hadamard product gives the same result.

These properties make the Hadamard product easy to manipulate when working with elementwise operations.

Let's look at a concrete example.
